title: Serum osmolality
subtitle: Calculated osmolality, tonicity and osmolal gap
summary: Calculated osmolality, tonicity and osmolal gap
introduction: Calculated osmolality is an estimate. Use measured serum osmolality when evaluating unexplained hyponatraemia, suspected toxic alcohol ingestion or a possible osmolal gap.

rows.name: Typical measured range
notes: Low measured osmolality with hyponatraemia confirms hypotonic hyponatraemia. Normal/high osmolality suggests glucose, mannitol or another effective osmole, or pseudohyponatraemia.

rows.name: Osmolal gap
notes: A raised gap can occur with toxic alcohols, ethanol, ketones, lactate, renal failure or laboratory/formula variation. A normal gap does not exclude late toxic alcohol poisoning.

calculations.title: Osmolal gap
interpretation: A raised gap can occur with toxic alcohols, ethanol, ketones, lactate, renal failure or formula/laboratory variation.

inputs.label: Measured osmolality (mOsm/kg)
inputs.validationMessage: Enter measured osmolality between 150 and 500 mOsm/kg.

inputs.label: Calculated osmolality (mOsm/kg)
inputs.validationMessage: Enter calculated osmolality between 150 and 500 mOsm/kg.

urgentFindings: Hyponatraemia with seizure, reduced consciousness, severe confusion or persistent vomiting.
Measured/calculated osmolality ≥320 mOsm/kg with profound dehydration or altered cognition: consider HHS.
Raised osmolal gap with visual symptoms, severe metabolic acidosis, renal injury or suspected methanol/ethylene glycol ingestion.
overrides: Use the reporting laboratory’s reference ranges and compare with previous results, symptoms, observations, medication and fluid status.

commonPatterns.title: True hypotonic hyponatraemia
interpretation: Confirms genuine hypotonic hyponatraemia rather than an artefact or an osmotically-driven dilution — this is the pattern that needs the standard hyponatraemia work-up (volume status, SIADH causes, medication review)
actions: Assess volume status and review medication, as for standard hyponatraemia assessment
Treat as time-critical if seizure, reduced consciousness, severe confusion or persistent vomiting are present (see urgent findings)
Correct cautiously — rapid correction of longstanding hyponatraemia carries a risk of osmotic demyelination

commonPatterns.title: Pseudohyponatraemia or an effective osmole
interpretation: A low sodium with a normal or high measured osmolality suggests either pseudohyponatraemia (severe hyperlipidaemia or hyperproteinaemia affecting the sodium assay) or an additional effective osmole such as glucose or mannitol drawing water into the vascular space
This is not true hypotonic hyponatraemia and does not need — and could be harmed by — standard hyponatraemia fluid correction
actions: Check glucose, as marked hyperglycaemia is a common and important cause of this pattern (see further testing)
Consider recent mannitol administration and severe lipid/protein abnormalities as alternative explanations
Avoid treating this as standard hypotonic hyponatraemia; address the underlying osmole (e.g. treat hyperglycaemia) instead

commonPatterns.title: Raised osmolal gap — possible toxic alcohol
findings: Osmolal gap raised (measured osmolality substantially exceeds calculated)
Visual symptoms, severe metabolic acidosis, renal injury, or a history of ingestion
interpretation: A raised osmolal gap can occur with toxic alcohols (methanol, ethylene glycol), ethanol, ketones, lactate, renal failure or formula/laboratory variation

A normal gap does not exclude late toxic alcohol poisoning — by the time acidosis develops, the parent alcohol has often been metabolised and the gap can have narrowed even as the patient deteriorates
actions: Treat as time-critical if there are visual symptoms, severe acidosis, renal injury or a history of suspected toxic alcohol ingestion (see urgent findings)
Request a venous blood gas and consider ethanol level to help interpret the gap (see further testing)
Do not be falsely reassured by a normal gap late in the course if the history strongly suggests toxic alcohol ingestion — discuss with poisons information/toxicology

commonPatterns.title: Hyperosmolar picture suggesting HHS
interpretation: Supports hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state; this carries a high mortality and needs a different fluid/insulin approach to DKA, with careful attention to the rate of osmolality correction
actions: Treat as time-critical and arrange urgent hospital assessment (see urgent findings)
Request glucose and ketones to distinguish HHS from DKA, noting that mixed pictures can occur (see further testing)
Assess for seizures, focal neurology and hypotension, and monitor closely as correction proceeds

rationale: Sodium and urea are needed to calculate osmolality and interpret hyponatraemia patterns; renal function is also relevant to a raised osmolal gap
Marked hyperglycaemia can raise measured osmolality and cause a dilutional (pseudo-)hyponatraemia, and is essential to distinguish HHS from other causes of a hyperosmolar state
Identifies metabolic acidosis that supports toxic alcohol ingestion or ketoacidosis as a cause of a raised osmolal gap
Ketones can raise the osmolal gap and help distinguish DKA/starvation ketosis from toxic alcohol ingestion as the cause of a raised gap
Ethanol itself raises the osmolal gap; knowing the level helps determine whether it fully explains a raised gap or whether a toxic alcohol should still be considered
Severe hyperlipidaemia or hyperproteinaemia can cause pseudohyponatraemia, which should be considered when sodium is low but measured osmolality is normal
